headline: Indigenous Languages Come Alive as Dragonflies Reveal Colombia's Hidden Waters
meta_description: Researchers and Indigenous communities in Guainía, Colombia discover 120 dragonfly species while reviving endangered native languages through collaborative sci…
summary_short: In remote Guainía, Colombia, Indigenous communities are recovering forgotten words while cataloging dragonflies—revealing both biodiversity and the health of local water…
body:
In the remote region of Guainía in eastern Colombia, a collaboration between scientific researchers and Indigenous communities has uncovered a remarkable double discovery: nearly 120 dragonfly species—twelve times more than the ten previously known to science—and a crucial opportunity to preserve languages at the edge of extinction. As researchers from the Dragones Guainía project worked to fill gaps in the scientific record, they realized that naming these insects in Spanish held little meaning for communities whose knowledge of the landscape had been shaped by entirely different ways of seeing the world. Some participants didn't even speak Spanish. The solution emerged organically: workshops where researchers displayed the dragonflies found in puddles, streams, and rivers while elders and young people alike tried to identify them in their own languages—Tucano, Curripaco, and Puinave, among others. Sometimes the ancestral names could be recovered from memory. Sometimes communities had to create them anew, breathing life back into languages themselves at risk of disappearing.

The work reveals something deeper than just biodiversity. Dragonflies and damselflies depend on healthy freshwater ecosystems, making them sensitive indicators of water quality. As Guainía—known as the land of many waters—faces mounting pressures from mining, deforestation, and poorly managed waste, these insects have become partners in understanding what is happening to the region's lifeblood. In the community of Remanso, members of the Puinave tribe created dragonfly names in an ancestral language while working to recover it. Delio Suárez, a Tucano Indigenous leader from the multiethnic community La Ceiba, captured the stakes: "This leaves us with the task of recovering their names, of looking back and asking the last remaining wisdom keepers that we have."

Today, Indigenous communities are developing their own monitoring systems for dragonflies and, through them, taking active stewardship of the waters they depend on—guided by words pulled back from the edge of silence.
quick_facts: Researchers found nearly 120 dragonfly species in Guainía, up from just 10 previously recorded
Indigenous communities in La Ceiba, Remanso, and other settlements participated in naming the insects
Guainía sits at the meeting point of the Amazon, Orinoco Basin, and Guyana Shield
Dragonflies serve as indicators of freshwater ecosystem health threatened by mining and deforestation
Communities created new names in Tucano, Puinave, and Curripaco languages to prevent extinction
